column1: Information since September points to a strong labor market and moderate growth, but soft business investment/exports and below-2% inflation led the FOMC to cut the funds rate to 1.5–1.75% and deploy ample-reserve operations (T-bill purchases and repos) to ensure smooth policy transmission. In line with Sims (1992) on U.S. monetary shocks affecting real activity, this easing should modestly support output in the short run. Consistent with Svensson’s work on inflation targeting, preemptive easing can help prevent inflation expectations from drifting lower when market-based compensation is subdued. The coexistence of low unemployment and muted inflation is also consistent with Christiano and Eichenbaum (1992b) and the broader labor-supply elasticity literature (e.g., Chari, Kehoe, and McGrattan), suggesting tight labor markets need not immediately translate into accelerating inflation. Overall, the stance is cautiously accommodative and slightly positive for the outlook, while acknowledging persistent uncertainties—an approach aligned with the Fed’s dual mandate and credibility built since the Volcker era. sentiment score = 0.25
